⟦p:habakkuk_1334|Habakkuk⟧ is a prophet who argues with God. Most prophetic books carry the Lord's word to the people. This one begins with the prophet's own complaint to the Lord, and much of it is a conversation between them, honest and urgent, about why God allows evil to go on. It ends with a prayer meant to be sung.

The book gives ⟦p:habakkuk_1334|Habakkuk⟧ only his name and his title, the prophet, and tells us nothing of his family, his home or his life. The setting, though, is clear. In the first chapter the Lord announces that he is raising up the Chaldeans, the people of southern ⟦l:mesopotamia_790|Mesopotamia⟧ better known to us as the Babylonians.

The listener has just heard ⟦p:nahum_2145|Nahum⟧ announce the fall of ⟦l:nineveh_899|Nineveh⟧. The power that brought it down was ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧. In six hundred and twenty-six before Christ a Chaldean leader named Nabopolassar seized the throne of Babylon and threw off Assyrian rule. With the ⟦l:media_776|Medes⟧ as allies, the Babylonians destroyed Nineveh in six hundred and twelve, and in six hundred and five Nabopolassar's son ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧ crushed the Egyptian army at Carchemish on the ⟦l:euphrates_421|Euphrates⟧. Within a few years the whole of the region, Judah included, lay at Babylon's feet.

⟦p:habakkuk_1334|Habakkuk⟧ spoke in these years, near the end of the seventh century before Christ. Judah was in turmoil. Good King ⟦p:josiah_1730|Josiah⟧, who had led a great reform of the nation's worship, had been killed in battle against ⟦p:pharaoh-nechoh_2337|Pharaoh Neco⟧ at ⟦l:megiddo_777|Megiddo⟧ in six hundred and nine. His son ⟦p:jehoiakim_1085|Jehoiakim⟧, placed on the throne by ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, was a harsh and grasping ruler, and ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧, who was prophesying in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ at the same time, condemned him for building his palace by injustice. The violence and corruption Habakkuk complains of in his first lines fit those years well.

The book has a clear and simple shape. ⟦p:habakkuk_1334|Habakkuk⟧ cries out about the injustice he sees in Judah, and the Lord answers that he is sending the Babylonians as his instrument of judgement. That answer only troubles the prophet more, for it seems to mean a holy God using a nation more wicked than the one it punishes. Habakkuk takes his stand on the watchtower to wait for a reply, and it comes as a vision to be written down plainly, together with a series of woes on the arrogant conqueror. Finally the prophet prays, recalling the Lord's mighty acts in the past, and resolves to trust him whatever comes.

One short line from the Lord's reply, the righteous will live by faith, would have a long history. The apostle ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ quotes it in his letters to the Romans and the Galatians, and it appears again in the letter to the Hebrews.
1:
The book begins with a cry. How long, O Lord, must I call for help, and you do not hear? ⟦p:habakkuk_1334|Habakkuk⟧ looks around him in Judah and sees violence, strife and injustice. The law is paralysed, the wicked hem in the righteous, and nothing seems to change. He has prayed for a long time.

The Lord's answer is not the one he expected. Look at the nations, the Lord says, for I am doing something in your days that you would not believe if you were told. He is raising up the Chaldeans, the Babylonians, a ruthless and impetuous nation that sweeps across the earth. They scoff at kings and laugh at fortresses, and their own strength is their god.

That only deepens ⟦p:habakkuk_1334|Habakkuk⟧'s distress, and his second complaint follows at once. The Lord's eyes are too pure to look on evil, he says, and yet he is silent while the wicked swallow those more righteous than themselves. He pictures the conqueror as a fisherman dragging nations in his net, and worshipping the net itself.
2:
⟦p:habakkuk_1334|Habakkuk⟧ has made his complaint, and now he waits, like a watchman at his post on the city wall, for the Lord's answer.

He is told to write the vision plainly on tablets, so that a herald can run with it. Its fulfilment may seem slow, but it will surely come. Then the Lord contrasts two kinds of people. The proud one, puffed up and never satisfied, gathers nations as greedily as death itself. But the righteous will live by faith.

The rest of the chapter is a taunt song that the conquered nations will one day sing over the conqueror. Five times it cries woe: on the plunderer whose creditors will suddenly rise against him, on the man who builds his house by unjust gain until the very stones cry out from the wall, on the city built with bloodshed, on the one who makes his neighbours drunk to gaze on their shame, and on the worshipper who calls to a block of wood, awake. In the middle of the woes stands a promise that the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the Lord's glory, and the chapter ends in silence before him.
3:
The book ends with a prayer, and it reads like a psalm. It has a heading with a musical term, Shigionoth, like the Shiggaion of the seventh psalm. It uses the word Selah, familiar from the Psalms, and it closes with a note for the choirmaster.

⟦p:habakkuk_1334|Habakkuk⟧ begins by asking the Lord to renew his great deeds in these years, and in wrath to remember mercy. Then he describes a vision of God coming in power from the south, from ⟦l:teman_1150|Teman⟧ and Mount ⟦l:paran_921|Paran⟧, the wilderness regions associated with ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧ and Edom. The imagery draws on Israel's oldest memories: plague and fever marching with him, ⟦l:midian_796|Midian⟧ trembling, the sea trampled, the sun and moon standing still, as in the days of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ and ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧.

The vision leaves the prophet shaking, yet he resolves to wait quietly for the day when distress will fall on the invaders. The book's final lines are his response. Even if the fig tree fails and the fields yield nothing, he will rejoice in the Lord.
